title: Signals and How Far They Travel

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: {{c1::Signal transduction}} is the process by which a cell converts a signal from outside into a change inside, in its behavior or in the genes it reads.
cards.quote: Signal transduction is the process by which a cell converts a signal from outside into a change inside, in its behavior or in the genes it reads.
cards.section: A message with no wire

cards.front: A {{c1::first messenger}} is the signal itself: the molecule or physical stimulus that arrives from outside before the cell has done anything with it.
cards.back: Example: secretin.
cards.quote: A first messenger is the signal itself, the molecule or physical stimulus that arrives from outside before the cell has done anything with it.
cards.section: A message with no wire

cards.front: In a dog, acid on the lining of a nerve-cut intestinal loop makes the pancreas secrete, and an extract of the lining injected into a vein does too. Why does the injection result rule out a local nerve reflex?
cards.back: The injection bypasses every gut nerve, yet the pancreas still secreted. Only a chemical from the gut lining (secretin) carried in the blood fits both results.
cards.quote: Something in the gut lining, later named secretin, was released by acid and carried to the pancreas in the blood.
cards.section: A message with no wire

cards.front: The vagus nerve of a beating frog heart is stimulated, slowing it. The salt solution bathing that heart is moved to a second heart, whose nerves are not stimulated, and it slows too. What does this show?
cards.back: The nerve acted by releasing a chemical (Vagusstoff, later identified as acetylcholine) that drifted to its target, not by passing a current.
cards.quote: A nerve cell had given an order by releasing a chemical that drifted to its target, not by passing a current.
cards.section: A message with no wire

cards.front: The average time one messenger molecule survives before it is destroyed or captured is its {{c1::lifetime, τ}}.
cards.back: How fast it wanders is its diffusion coefficient, D.
cards.quote: Sooner or later every messenger is destroyed or captured, and the average time one molecule survives is its lifetime, τ (tau).
cards.section: Three questions and one idea

cards.front: For a messenger that diffuses and is cleared by first-order removal, the steady gradient has a decay length of about {{c1::√(D × τ)}}.
cards.back: D is the diffusion coefficient and τ the messenger's lifetime. This is the 'reach' of the signal.
cards.quote: the steady gradient has a decay length of about √(D × τ)
cards.section: Three questions and one idea

cards.front: After a diffusing messenger's release stops, on what timescale does its concentration fall, and how long does building its gradient out to the decay length take?
cards.back: It falls on the timescale τ, and building the gradient out to its decay length also takes on the order of τ.
cards.why: So lifetime buys reach but costs tempo.
cards.quote: After release stops, its concentration falls on the timescale τ; building the gradient out to its decay length also takes on the order of τ.
cards.section: Three questions and one idea

cards.front: Why is lengthening a diffusing messenger's lifetime a poor way to buy reach?
cards.back: The decay time grows in step with lifetime (τ), while reach grows only as its square root (√τ).
cards.quote: the decay time grows in step with lifetime, while reach grows only as its square root
cards.section: Three questions and one idea

cards.front: Which modes of signaling can the rule 'lifetime buys reach and costs tempo' describe, how do blood-borne hormones differ, and which lie outside it?
cards.back: It can describe autocrine, paracrine and synaptic signals when transport is mainly diffusion and removal is roughly first-order. Blood flow, not √(D × τ), sets a hormone's range, though clearance still helps set how fast its level falls after secretion stops. Contact modes lie outside this extracellular diffusion-clearance rule.
cards.quote: Blood flow carries endocrine signals, so √(D × τ) does not set their range, although clearance still helps set how quickly their concentration falls after secretion stops.
cards.section: Three questions and one idea

cards.front: Why does diffusion become so slow over long distances?
cards.back: Diffusion is a random walk, so the typical time to wander a distance grows with the square of that distance (t ≈ x²/2D).
cards.quote: Because diffusion is a random walk, and the typical time to wander a distance grows with the square of that distance.
cards.section: Diffusion punishes distance

cards.front: A small molecule has D = 10^-5 cm²/s. Using t = x²/(2D), how long does it take to diffuse 1 mm?
cards.back: x = 0.1 cm, x² = 0.01 cm². 2D = 2 × 10^-5 cm²/s. t = 0.01 / (2 × 10^-5) = 500 s, about eight minutes.
cards.quote: t = 0.01 / (2 × 10^-5) = 500 s, about eight minutes.
cards.section: Diffusion punishes distance

cards.front: A small molecule diffuses 1 mm in about eight minutes. How long does it take to diffuse 1 cm, and why is the answer not eighty minutes?
cards.back: About fourteen hours. Ten times the distance costs 10² = 100 times the time, because diffusion time grows with distance squared.
cards.quote: About fourteen hours, not eighty minutes: ten times the distance costs 10² = 100 times the time.
cards.section: Diffusion punishes distance

cards.front: A small molecule (D = 10^-5 cm²/s) must act within one minute. Using x = √(2Dt), how far can it diffuse, and what does that imply for hormones?
cards.back: x = √(2 × 10^-5 × 60) cm ≈ 0.035 cm, about 350 µm. Past a few hundred micrometers diffusion is too slow, so hormones ride the blood, which circulates around the body in about a minute.
cards.quote: Past a few hundred micrometers, diffusion cannot deliver a message that has to act within a minute.
cards.section: Diffusion punishes distance

cards.front: In three dimensions, t ≈ x²/6D. How long does a small molecule (D = 10^-5 cm²/s) take to reach 1 mm, and does this change the conclusion of the one-dimensional estimate?
cards.back: t = 0.01 / (6 × 10^-5) ≈ 170 s, about three minutes, three times sooner. The conclusion stands: time still grows with the square of distance.
cards.quote: In three dimensions a molecule reaches a given distance about three times sooner, t ≈ x²/6D.
cards.section: Diffusion in three dimensions

cards.front: What is juxtacrine signaling?
cards.back: Contact signaling in which a ligand anchored in one cell's membrane binds a receptor on the cell pressed against it. The contact is the address.
cards.quote: In juxtacrine signaling, a ligand (a molecule that binds a receptor) is anchored in one cell's membrane and binds a receptor on the cell pressed against it.
cards.section: Five modes, five answers to the same physics

cards.front: What is autocrine signaling, and what does it let a cell do?
cards.back: The cell releases a signal that binds receptors on its own surface. It lets the cell reinforce its own decision.
cards.quote: The cell releases a signal that binds receptors on its own surface, which lets a cell reinforce its own decision.
cards.section: Five modes, five answers to the same physics

cards.front: {{c1::Histamine}} released during inflammation is the standard example of a paracrine signal.
cards.quote: Histamine released during inflammation is the standard example.
cards.section: Five modes, five answers to the same physics

cards.front: Synaptic signaling is described as paracrine signaling built for speed and privacy. What gives it each?
cards.back: A gap only tens of nanometers wide, so the message arrives almost at once and acts mostly on the cell across it, plus fast clearance.
cards.quote: This is a paracrine signal with the geometry built for speed and privacy
cards.section: Five modes, five answers to the same physics

cards.front: What is volume transmission?
cards.back: Release of a transmitter, such as serotonin, away from a tight synapse so that it drifts farther to receptors.
cards.quote: Some transmitters, serotonin among them, are often released away from a tight synapse and drift farther, a pattern called volume transmission.
cards.section: Five modes, five answers to the same physics

cards.front: An endocrine hormone reaches every cell the blood reaches. What keeps its message from the wrong cells?
cards.back: Not the route. Mainly which cells carry the receptor.
cards.why: Secretin shows that a hormone need not come from a gland: it comes from cells in the gut lining.
cards.quote: A cell, often but not always in a gland, releases a hormone, a signal carried in the blood, and every cell the blood reaches is exposed to it.
cards.section: Five modes, five answers to the same physics

cards.front: A secreted protein in water has D = 10^-6 cm²/s and survives τ = 100 s. About how far does it reach?
cards.back: D × τ = 10^-4 cm². √(10^-4 cm²) = 10^-2 cm = 100 µm, about five to ten cell diameters.
cards.quote: D × τ = 10^-4 cm², and √(10^-4 cm²) = 10^-2 cm = 100 µm, about five to ten cell diameters.
cards.section: Lifetime buys reach and costs tempo

cards.front: A growth factor reaches about 100 µm from its source. A mutation makes each molecule survive nine times longer. Predict the new reach and how long the wider gradient takes to build.
cards.back: Reach triples to about 300 µm (√9 = 3). Build time rises about ninefold, because it scales with lifetime itself.
cards.quote: Three times the reach costs nine times the time.
cards.section: Lifetime buys reach and costs tempo

cards.front: Why is a secreted protein's diffusion coefficient in tissue lower than in water?
cards.back: Binding to matrix and to receptors slows its spread: a molecule stuck part of the time covers less ground. The water value of 10^-6 cm²/s is an upper bound.
cards.quote: Binding to matrix and to receptors slows a protein's spread, because a molecule that is stuck part of the time covers less ground.
cards.section: Lifetime buys reach and costs tempo

cards.front: Holding lifetime fixed, D falls a thousandfold, from 10^-6 cm²/s (water) to 10^-9 cm²/s (sticky tissue). By what factor does reach fall, and what change in lifetime would do the same?
cards.back: Reach ∝ √D, so it falls by √1000 ≈ 32, about thirtyfold. A thousandfold drop in lifetime would do the same.
cards.quote: At the slow end every reach is about thirty times smaller (√1000 ≈ 32), as much as a thousandfold drop in lifetime would cause.
cards.section: Lifetime buys reach and costs tempo

cards.front: Acetylcholinesterase removes acetylcholine within about 1 ms. For a small molecule (D = 10^-5 cm²/s), about how far does acetylcholine reach?
cards.back: √(D × τ) = √(10^-5 × 10^-3) cm = 10^-4 cm, about 1 µm. This is only an order-of-magnitude scale, not a literal boundary (the cleft is thin, the enzyme is not uniform, its kinetics can saturate), but rapid clearance still helps make the signal brief and limit spillover.
cards.quote: Substituting a small-molecule D and that effective lifetime gives √(D × τ) = √(10^-5 × 10^-3) cm, about 1 µm.
cards.section: Lifetime buys reach and costs tempo

cards.front: Epinephrine's half-life in blood is about 2.5 minutes. What fraction remains ten minutes after the adrenal gland stops releasing it?
cards.back: 10 / 2.5 = 4 half-lives, so (1/2)^4 = 1/16, about 6%. With a 3-minute half-life about 10% remains: a tenth or less.
cards.why: So a hormone level can track changes over minutes, not seconds.
cards.quote: epinephrine in roughly two to three minutes, so ten minutes after the adrenal gland stops releasing it, about a tenth or less remains
cards.section: Lifetime buys reach and costs tempo

cards.front: Why do many hormone receptors bind at low concentrations, and why do many surface-receptor pathways amplify what they detect?
cards.back: Once mixed through the circulation, a hormone is spread through about five liters of blood (about three of plasma), so it is dilute. Many pathways amplify the signal, often through second messengers.
cards.quote: Once mixed through the circulation, a hormone is distributed through about five liters of blood (about three of plasma), although its effective distribution volume depends on the hormone.
cards.section: Lifetime buys reach and costs tempo

cards.front: A cell divides only when a neighbor sends it a short-lived paracrine growth factor. A mutation makes the cell produce that factor itself while it still carries the receptor. Predict its behavior and why this is dangerous.
cards.back: It forms an autocrine loop, which can reduce its dependence on a neighbor's signal and contribute to inappropriate proliferation, weakening the constraint that short reach and short life provide. Example: v-sis encodes a form of PDGF's B chain, driving transformed cells through their own PDGF receptors.
cards.quote: A cell that makes a growth factor and carries its receptor has created an autocrine loop, which can reduce its dependence on growth signals from neighboring cells and contribute to inappropriate proliferation.
cards.section: Lifetime buys reach and costs tempo

cards.front: A paracrine factor that an extracellular enzyme destroys in seconds becomes enzyme-resistant and survives for hours. Predict the effects on its range, on which cells respond, and on how quickly its level can change.
cards.back: Range grows (as √τ), so distant receptor-bearing cells now respond and the signal is no longer local. Its level also falls and builds more slowly, because decay time scales with τ.
cards.why: Rests on reach ≈ √(D × τ) for diffusion with first-order clearance, and on decay time ≈ τ.
cards.quote: Either way, a paracrine signal stays local because its neighborhood destroys it, captures it or slows its spread.
cards.section: Lifetime buys reach and costs tempo

cards.front: Name the routes by which cells clear a messenger, each of which sets τ.
cards.back: Enzymes destroy it; transporters pump it back into the sender or into glia; blood flow carries it off (or, from a small space such as a synaptic gap, diffusion out of the gap).
cards.quote: One way cells end signals is by clearing the messenger, and each route of clearance is a way of setting τ.
cards.section: Ending the message: clearance sets τ

cards.front: Why must acetylcholinesterase clear acetylcholine from the nerve-muscle gap within about a millisecond?
cards.back: If the transmitter lingered, the next message could not be told apart from the last, so the gap must be wiped clean after every impulse.
cards.quote: if the transmitter lingered, the next message could not be told apart from the last
cards.section: Ending the message: clearance sets τ

cards.front: Eserine blocks acetylcholinesterase. What happens to acetylcholine's lifetime at the synapse, and what does the synapse gain and lose?
cards.back: Lifetime rises, so each release acts longer (the gain). The cost is tempo: the gap is not wiped clean between impulses, so messages blur. Reach grows only as √τ.
cards.quote: The cost is tempo: the gap is no longer wiped clean after each impulse, so the next message is harder to tell from the last.
cards.section: Ending the message: clearance sets τ

cards.front: Fluoxetine, an SSRI, blocks the transporter that pumps serotonin back into the sending neuron. What happens to serotonin's lifetime in the gap, and why does this alone not explain the drug's benefit in depression?
cards.back: Serotonin lingers longer and keeps its receptors occupied longer, within hours. The benefit takes weeks and is thought to come from slower brain changes that follow.
cards.quote: Its benefit in depression takes weeks to appear and is thought to come from slower changes in the brain that follow
cards.section: Ending the message: clearance sets τ

cards.front: A nerve agent blocks acetylcholinesterase at the nerve-muscle junction. The motor nerve fires a rapid train of impulses. Predict what the muscle does and why.
cards.back: Acetylcholine lingers, so the gap is not wiped clean and each impulse is harder to tell from the last; the muscle stays contracted longer. Rule: lifetime costs tempo.
cards.why: The same enzyme is the target of some Alzheimer's drugs, which prolong acetylcholine by the same route.
cards.quote: Acetylcholinesterase sits in the gap between nerve and muscle, and its millisecond speed is the point
cards.section: Ending the message: clearance sets τ

cards.front: A hormone in the blood reaches nearly every organ. What decides which cells respond, and how?
cards.back: The receptor, not the signal. A cell without the receptor ignores the signal, and cells with different receptors for the same molecule respond differently.
cards.why: Acetylcholine slows the heart but contracts skeletal muscle, because they carry different receptors.
cards.quote: The receptor, not the signal, sets who responds.
cards.section: Who answers: the receptor

cards.front: A drug blocks the epinephrine receptor on heart cells only. The adrenal gland then releases epinephrine. Predict the responses of liver, fat and heart.
cards.back: Liver still breaks down glycogen and fat cells still break down fat; the heart's beat does not strengthen. The hormone reaches all three, but the receptor decides who answers.
cards.quote: Epinephrine, a hormone from the adrenal gland, drives glycogen breakdown in liver cells, fat breakdown in fat cells and a stronger beat in the heart
cards.section: Who answers: the receptor

cards.front: Why does estradiol behave more like O2 and NO than like the peptide hormone ghrelin, even though both estradiol and ghrelin are hormones?
cards.back: A hormone is defined by how it travels, in the blood, not by its chemistry. Estradiol is uncharged and fat-soluble, so it crosses membranes like O2 and NO.
cards.why: So sort first messengers by whether they cross, not by category.
cards.quote: A hormone is defined by how it travels, in the blood, not by what it is made of
cards.section: Can the messenger cross? Where the receptor sits

cards.front: Glucose is small and uncharged; estradiol is larger, with four fused carbon rings. Which crosses the lipid core of the membrane on its own, and why?
cards.back: Estradiol, which has almost no charged groups. Glucose is covered in polar hydroxyl groups and needs a transporter.
cards.why: Charge and polarity decide, not size alone.
cards.quote: Charge and polarity decide, not size alone.
cards.section: Can the messenger cross? Where the receptor sits

cards.front: Acetylcholine and epinephrine are both small molecules. Predict whether either crosses the lipid bilayer on its own, and where their receptors must sit.
cards.back: Neither crosses. Acetylcholine's nitrogen carries a permanent positive charge and epinephrine's amine is positively charged at body pH, so both need a protein in the membrane, for these two a surface receptor.
cards.quote: the nitrogen of acetylcholine carries a permanent positive charge, and the amine of epinephrine is positively charged at body pH
cards.section: Can the messenger cross? Where the receptor sits

cards.front: O2, CO2 and NO slip through the lipid core of the membrane, and so does the steroid {{c1::estradiol}}.
cards.back: Its main receptor is inside the cell.
cards.quote: O2, CO2 and NO slip through, and so does estradiol.
cards.section: Can the messenger cross? Where the receptor sits

cards.front: Two new first messengers are found: one small, uncharged and fat-soluble; the other a charged peptide. Predict where each one's receptor most likely sits, and why.
cards.back: The fat-soluble one can cross the bilayer, so its receptor may sit inside the cell. The charged peptide cannot cross, so it needs a surface receptor (or a channel or transporter).
cards.why: Rests on the rule that crossing predicts where the receptor sits.
cards.quote: Whether a messenger can cross predicts where its receptor sits.
cards.section: Can the messenger cross? Where the receptor sits

cards.front: Every liver cell in the body must release glucose within a minute. Choose a mode of signaling, defend it, and name its cost.
cards.back: Endocrine: a hormone such as adrenaline in the blood reaches every liver cell in about a minute, while diffusion would need hours per centimeter. Receptor relays amplify the dilute hormone. Cost: every other cell with the receptor answers too.
cards.quote: The blood reaches every liver cell within about a minute, while diffusion would need hours to cover even a centimeter.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Only the cell next door should divide. Choose a mode of signaling, defend it, and say why endocrine signaling would be wrong.
cards.back: Juxtacrine, so the contact is the address; or, for a small neighborhood, a quickly destroyed paracrine factor with √(D × τ) of a cell diameter or two. Endocrine would reach every cell carrying the receptor.
cards.quote: An endocrine signal would be wrong here: through the blood, a command to divide reaches every cell that carries the receptor.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Acetylcholine released by a nerve was destroyed before any chemical test could detect it. How did Dale and Feldberg detect it?
cards.back: They added eserine, which protects acetylcholine and sensitizes leech muscle, and used the height of the leech muscle's slow contraction, compared with known amounts, as the measure.
cards.quote: The height of the leech muscle's slow contraction, read against contractions from known amounts, became the measurement.
cards.section: Catching acetylcholine with a leech muscle
